content: 1. A community should carefully evaluate these recommendations and establish its own tailored response plan before the emergence of a suicide cluster. 2. The response to a suicide crisis must involve all relevant sectors of the community and should be coordinated by a designated committee. 3. A Coordinating Committee should be formed to manage the day-to-day response to the crisis. 4. A Host Agency should be identified to oversee the response plan, monitor the incidence of suicide, and convene meetings of the Coordinating Committee as needed. 5. If the response plan is to be implemented, the first step should involve contacting and preparing the groups that will play critical roles in the initial days of the response. 6. The response should be conducted in a way that avoids glorifying the suicide victims and minimizes sensationalism. 7. Individuals at high risk of suicide should be identified and provided with at least one screening interview by a trained counselor. These individuals should be referred for further counseling or other services as necessary. 8. Accurate and appropriate information should be provided to the media in a timely manner. 9. Environmental factors that may increase the likelihood of further suicides or suicide attempts should be identified and addressed. 10. Long-term issues suggested by the nature of the suicide cluster should be systematically addressed. 11. Recent suicide clusters among teenagers and young adults have garnered national attention, highlighting growing public concern about this issue. 12. Unfortunately, our understanding of the causes and prevention of suicide clusters remains incomplete. 13. A suicide cluster is defined as a group of suicides or suicide attempts that occur closer together in time and space than would normally be expected in a given community. 14. Statistical analysis of national mortality data indicates that clusters of completed suicides predominantly occur among adolescents and young adults, accounting for approximately 1%-5% of all suicides in this age group. 15. Suicide clusters are often thought to occur through a process of contagion, although this hypothesis has not been formally tested. 16. Anecdotal evidence suggests that suicides occurring later in a cluster are often influenced by earlier suicides within the same cluster. 17. 18. The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) has assisted several state and local health departments in investigating and responding to apparent clusters of suicide and suicide attempts. 19. These clusters have created a crisis atmosphere in affected communities, generating intense concern among parents, students, school officials, and others. 20. Community leaders faced the dual challenge of preventing the cluster from expanding while managing the existing crisis. 21. Opportunities for prevention were often missed during the early stages of response as community leaders sought guidance on how best to address suicide clusters. 22. The recommendations in this report were developed to assist community leaders in public health, mental health, education, and other fields in creating a community response plan for suicide clusters or situations that might develop into clusters. 23. A workshop to develop these recommendations was jointly sponsored by the New Jersey State Department of Health and the CDC in November 1987 in Newark, New Jersey. 24. Participants in the workshop included individuals who had played key roles in community responses to nine different suicide clusters, representing sectors such as education, medicine, local government, community mental health, crisis centers, and state public health and mental health agencies. 25. Representatives from the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), the Indian Health Service (IHS), the American Association of Suicidology (AAS), and the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO) also participated. 26. These recommendations are not intended as explicit instructions for every community but rather as a conceptual framework for developing response plans tailored to the specific needs, resources, and cultural characteristics of each community. 27. The recommendations will be periodically revised to reflect new knowledge in suicide prevention and lessons learned from implementing this plan. 28. Certain elements of the proposed plan for preventing and containing suicide clusters differ significantly from crisis-response plans for other community emergencies, primarily due to the potentially contagious nature of suicidal behavior and the stigma and guilt often associated with suicide. 29. Other elements of the proposed plan are relevant to crisis-response plans in general. 30. State and local health planners should consider whether the plan they develop from these recommendations should be integrated into existing guidelines for managing other emergencies or mental health crises. 31. A community should review these recommendations and develop its own response plan before the onset of a suicide cluster. 32. When a suicide cluster is occurring or appears imminent, several steps in the recommended response plan should be implemented immediately. 33. For a timely reaction to be possible, the response plan must already be developed, agreed upon, and understood by all participants at the onset of the crisis. 34. The recommended response requires extensive coordination among various sectors of the community, which can be challenging even under normal circumstances and more so during a crisis. 35. In the early days of an evolving suicide cluster, there is often confusion and a sense of urgency in the community to take action to prevent additional suicides, but initial efforts are usually poorly coordinated. 36. Community members often disagree on the best course of action to prevent the cluster from expanding. 37. Communities typically develop a coordinated response plan during the crisis, but opportunities for prevention are often missed in the critical first hours of the response. 38. The response to the crisis should involve all concerned sectors of the community and be coordinated as follows: Individuals from relevant agencies (education, public health, mental health, local government, suicide crisis centers, etc.) should serve on a Coordinating Committee responsible for deciding when to implement the response plan and coordinating its execution. One agency should be designated as the host agency for the plan, with responsibilities including convening the Coordinating Committee, maintaining the response plan, and revising it periodically to reflect new knowledge and community changes. 39. Every effort should be made to promote and implement the proposed plan as a community endeavor, as no single agency has the resources or expertise to adequately respond to an evolving suicide cluster. 40. 41. The notification mechanism for identifying a potentially evolving suicide cluster should be tailored to the community's size and characteristics. 42. The response plan should be implemented under either of the following conditions: When a suicide cluster occurs in the community, defined as suicides or attempts occurring closer together in time and space than usual for the community. When one or more traumatic deaths occur in the community that may influence others to attempt or complete suicide. 43. It is difficult to explicitly define a suicide cluster, as the number and closeness of cases vary depending on the community's size and baseline suicide incidence. 44. When a community perceives it is facing a suicide cluster, steps should be taken to prevent further suicides that may be influenced by the crisis atmosphere or contagion. 45. In several suicide clusters, the crisis was preceded by one or more traumatic deaths among the community's youth, whether intentional or unintentional. 46. The hypothesis that a traumatic death can kindle a suicide cluster, regardless of its intentionality, has not been formally tested but is supported by anecdotal evidence. 47. The fear of a contagious effect of suicide is not the only reason to implement this plan; for example, a suicide cluster related to a common-source problem, such as economic downturns, would also warrant a response. 48. Whether and when to implement the response plan should be determined by the Coordinating Committee, relying on prudent judgments by community leaders. 49. If the response plan is to be implemented, the first step should be to contact and prepare the various groups identified in the plan. 50. 51. The crisis response should avoid glorifying the suicide victims and minimize sensationalism to prevent further suicides. 52. Community spokespersons should present an accurate picture of the deceased to students, parents, family, media, and others. 53. If suicides occur among school-aged individuals, the deaths should be announced in a manner that provides maximal support for students while minimizing hysteria. 54. Community spokespersons should avoid glorifying or vilifying the deceased, as either approach can have harmful consequences. 55. Persons at high risk should be identified and provided with at least one screening interview by a trained counselor, with referrals for further counseling or services as needed. 56. 57. Strategies to identify associates of the deceased or others at increased risk might include monitoring funeral attendees, hospital visitors, and school absentees. 58. Consider establishing hotlines or walk-in suicide crisis centers if they do not already exist in the community. 59. Provide counselors at specific sites, such as schools or community centers, and announce their availability to those affected by the recent deaths. 60. Enlist the local media to publish sources of help, such as hotlines, crisis centers, and community meetings.
